title: Many exiles, one people
hookLine: Moroccan, Iraqi, Yemenite, European and Ethiopian Jews meet in one country

cards: Which tune is the right one for grace after meals? On one street in a small Israeli town, it depends on the window. From one, a Moroccan grandmother's Arabic.

From the next, Yiddish. Across the road, a Yemenite family singing grace after meals to a tune the neighbors have never heard. Down the block, in later years, Amharic, from families who came from Ethiopia.
Every one of them says the same Hebrew blessings. They don't all sing them the same way.

teach.b: The prayer book had asked for this for a long time. In the weekday Amidah, the standing prayer, one blessing asks God to sound the great shofar for freedom and gather the exiles from the four corners of the earth.
Isaiah had said something close: God will gather the scattered of Judah from the four corners of the earth. The Hebrew name for that hope is kibbutz galuyot, the ingathering of the exiles.
Then it began to happen, and it was messier than a prayer. Families arrived from many countries. Some lived for a time in crowded transit camps of tents and huts.
Some newcomers from the Middle East and North Africa have said they were looked down on, sent to far-off towns, told their customs were old-fashioned.

Ethiopian Jews, who had kept their own long-held ways, met questions about whether they belonged at all. Those wounds are part of the story, and Israelis still argue about them. And yet the tables changed.
Moroccan families opened their doors for Mimouna, the night Passover ends, with sweet pancakes for anyone who walked in. Yemenite melodies found their way into popular Israeli songs.

The Ethiopian festival of Sigd, a day of longing for Jerusalem, came to be marked by the state. A psalm says it plainly: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is For brethren to dwell together in unity!"
Unity there doesn't have to mean sameness: different chants for the same Torah verses, different foods on the same Shabbat.
It can mean living side by side, and staying.

how: Jews pray for the ingathering of the exiles in a blessing of the weekday Amidah, and in Israel communities from different lands keep their own melodies and customs, such as the Moroccan Mimouna and the Ethiopian Sigd.

games.q: you are a Moroccan family, new in a town where nobody knows your customs. Passover ends tonight. what do you do?
o: keep the evening quiet, behind closed doors.
drop the old custom to fit in.
open the door with sweet food for anyone who comes.
games.why: at Mimouna, Moroccan families open their homes as Passover ends, with sweet pancakes for anyone who walks in.

practice: If there's something near you to eat, a date, a piece of bread, a spoon of honey, eat it slowly and wonder where it traveled from.
If not, bring back a dish someone else's family once served you at their table: the smell, the first bite, who was sitting there. Think of the hands that carried that recipe across a border.

wordCard.voice: Many exiles. Jews from Morocco, Iraq, Yemen, Europe, Ethiopia and beyond, gathered in one country, each bringing their own ways.
